The patriotic song "Sare Jahan Se Achha Hindustan Hamara" (also known as "Tarana-e-Hindi") was written by the poet Muhammad Iqbal (Allama Iqbal). It was first published in the weekly journal Ittehad on August 16, 1904.

Explanation of Other Options:

• Chandrasekhar Azad: A prominent Indian revolutionary and freedom fighter.

• Rabindranath Tagore: A Nobel laureate, poet, philosopher, and composer who wrote India's national anthem, "Jana Gana Mana."

• Sardar Bhagat Singh: A charismatic Indian revolutionary and socialist who was a key figure in the Indian independence movement.

Further insights:

• Muhammad Iqbal (1877 - 1938) was an influential poet, philosopher, and politician in British India.

• "Sare Jahan Se Achha" quickly gained popularity and became an anthem of opposition to British rule in India.

• While Iqbal later became a prominent advocate for the creation of Pakistan, this early poem remains a widely cherished patriotic song in India.

• Matangini Hazra was an Indian revolutionary who participated in the Indian independence movement until she was shot dead by the British Indian police in front of the Tamluk Police Station on 29 September 1942.

• She was affectionately known as Gandhi buri, Bengali for old lady Gandhi.

Dadabhai Naoroji, also known as the Grand Old Man of India, developed the Drain of Wealth Theory, which explained how Britain drained India's economic resources through:

I. Unfair trade practices - raw materials were exported cheaply, and finished goods were sold at high prices.

II. Salaries of British officials - paid from Indian revenues.

III. Home Charges - remittances sent to Britain.

His book "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India" provided statistical proof of this economic exploitation.

The Individual Satyagraha (1940) was launched by Mahatma Gandhi as a non-violent protest against British policies during World War II.

· It was different from mass movements like the Quit India Movement (1942) and was limited to select leaders.

· Vinoba Bhave was the first Satyagrahi, followed by Jawaharlal Nehru as the second Satyagrahi.

· Nehru was arrested on 31 October 1940 for delivering anti-war speeches and demanding freedom of speech.

· Other notable leaders arrested during Individual Satyagraha:

o Brahma Dutt (Third Satyagrahi)

o Acharya Kripalani

o J.B. Kripalani

Thus, the correct answer is Jawaharlal Nehru.

Annie Besant stated in 1902 that India was not ruled for its benefit, but rather for the benefit of its conquerors.

She was a prominent British social reformer and political activist who played a significant role in the Indian independence movement.

Explanation of Other Options:

• Bal Gangadhar Tilak: A prominent assertive nationalist leader, very critical of British rule.

• Lala Lajpat Rai: Another key assertive nationalist leader, also a strong critic of British economic exploitation.

• Sarojini Naidu: A prominent poet and political activist who became deeply involved in the independence movement, but her most active political phase was slightly later.

Further insights:

• Annie Besant's work through the Theosophical Society and her later political activism through the Home Rule League aimed to awaken Indian pride and demand self-governance.

• Her critique of British rule often focused on its detrimental impact on Indian culture, economy, and self-respect.

• If this specific quote is attributed to her in 1902, it would be an early expression of her strong pro-Indian and anti-colonial stance.

C. Rajagopalachari was a prominent leader in Indian politics, serving as the first Indian Governor General of India and a senior figure in the Congress party. He later founded the Swatantra Party, advocating for economic liberalism and individual freedom. However, he was not the first recipient of the Padma Shree Award.
The title "Father of the Nation" was given to Mahatma Gandhi by Subhas Chandra Bose, who was a prominent Indian nationalist leader and a key figure in the Indian independence movement.
Dadabhai Naoroji, an Indian nationalist, social reformer, and early leader in the Indian independence movement, is often credited with discussing and popularizing the concept of a "poverty line."

• Annie Besant was a prominent British social reformer, theosophist, and Indian nationalist.

• In 1916, she founded the Indian Home Rule League, advocating for self-governance (Home Rule) for India within the British Empire.

• She worked closely with Indian leaders and played a key role in mobilizing public opinion for the cause of Indian autonomy.

• She also became the first woman President of the Indian National Congress in 1917.

Other Options Explained:

• Maria Rye: British social reformer known for her work with orphaned children and emigration schemes to Canada, not connected to Indian politics.

• Catherine Osler: A British suffragist and women's rights activist, focused on British women's suffrage, not Indian independence.

• Anne Knight: An early British feminist and anti-slavery campaigner, predating Annie Besant, not involved in Indian nationalist movements.

Further Insight:

• The Indian Home Rule League movement was inspired by the Irish Home Rule movement.

• Along with Annie Besant, Bal Gangadhar Tilak also led a parallel Home Rule League in western India.

• The movement laid the groundwork for more assertive nationalist activities that followed, including the Non-Cooperation Movement led by Gandhi.

Top of Form

During the Quit India Movement in 1942, Mahatma Gandhi gave the iconic 'Do or Die' slogan, urging the Indian people to adopt a decisive and unwavering stance against British colonial rule. The slogan became a rallying cry for the intensification of the independence struggle.

· Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel is called the "Iron Man of India" due to his role in unifying the princely states into the Indian Union.

· He was instrumental in integrating over 560 princely states after independence.

· The title symbolizes his strength, determination, and firm leadership.

Further insights:

Grand Old Man of India - Dadabhai Naoroji

· He was one of the earliest Indian political leaders and a strong advocate for Indian self-rule.

· First Indian to be elected to the British Parliament.

· Known for his work on the Drain Theory, highlighting how British policies were economically exploiting India.

Raja Ram Mohan Roy

· A social and educational reformer, often considered the father of the Indian Renaissance.

· Advocated for the abolition of sati, child marriage, and promoted women's education and modern education.

· Founded the Brahmo Samaj in 1828.

Father of Indian Unrest - Bal Gangadhar Tilak

· A prominent freedom fighter and nationalist leader.

· Known for his assertive style of leadership and the slogan: "Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it."

· The British colonial authorities gave him this title due to his powerful and fiery speeches that stirred political awakening.

questions.question: Lal Bahadur Shastri was born on _________. लाल बहादुर शास्त्री का जन्म _________ को हुआ था।
questions.solution: Lal Bahadur Shastri, born on 2 October 1904, was a prominent Indian politician and statesman. He served as the second Prime Minister of India from 1964 to 1966, succeeding Jawaharlal Nehru. Shastri is remembered for his leadership during the Indo-Pakistani War of 1965 and for popularizing the slogan "Jai Jawan Jai Kisan" (Hail the Soldier, Hail the Farmer) to boost morale and emphasize the importance of both the military and agriculture in nation-building.

At the Lahore Session of the Indian National Congress in 1929, Jawaharlal Nehru, as the President, passed the resolution for Purna Swaraj (Complete Independence) and declared 26th January 1930 as Independence Day.

Shaukat Ali was one of the leaders who was instrumental in convincing Mahatma Gandhi about the need to start a non-cooperation movement in support of The Khilafat.

Khilafat movemen was a pan-Islamic force in India that arose in 1919 in an effort to salvage the Ottoman caliph as a symbol of unity among the Muslim community in India during the British raj. The movement was initially bolstered by Gandhi's noncooperation movement but fell apart after the abolition of the caliphate in 1924.

The combined Khilafat Non-Cooperation movement was the first all-India agitation against British rule.

Veer Surendra Sai (23 January 1809 - 28 February 1884) was a native Indian as well as a regional freedom fighter from the Bengal Presidency, now Odisha. He fought against British rule in India after they dethroned the king and queen of Sambalpur State as he was the legal heir.

questions.solution:
· Faraizi Movement: This socio-religious reform movement in Eastern Bengal in the early 19th century was founded by IV. Haji Shariatullah.

· Mohammedan Literary Society: Founded in Calcutta in 1863 to promote modern education and discuss political, social, and religious issues among Muslims, its founder was III. Nawab Abdul Latif.

· Indian Patriotic Association: This was founded by II. Sir Syed Ahmad Khan in 1888, along with Raja Shiv Prasad of Benaras, to counter the propaganda of the Indian National Congress and promote loyalty to the British.

· Wahabi Movement (also known as Tariqah-i-Muhammadiyah in India): This revivalist Islamic movement in India in the 19th century was significantly led and popularized by I. Sayyid Ahmad of Rae Bareli (also known as Syed Ahmed Barelvi).

Further insights:

• Faraizi Movement: Focused on adherence to the obligatory duties (faraiz) of Islam and opposed un-Islamic customs. It also had an agrarian character, fighting for the rights of peasants.

• Mohammedan Literary Society: Played a crucial role in the intellectual awakening of Muslims in Bengal by encouraging Western education alongside religious learning.

• Indian Patriotic Association: Formed to oppose the Indian National Congress and demonstrate Muslim loyalty to British rule, reflecting Sir Syed Ahmad Khan's political stance at the time.

• Wahabi Movement: Aimed to purify Islam and return to its original principles. It had both religious and political dimensions, including armed struggle against the Sikhs and later the British.

· The Bombay Presidency Association was founded in 1885 by:

o Badruddin Tyabji (first Muslim INC president)

o Pherozeshah Mehta (Indian nationalist leader)

o K.T. Telang (jurist and social reformer)

· It aimed to protect the rights of Indians under British rule.

· Tyabji was also the first Muslim president of the Indian National Congress.

Khudai Khidmatgar (Servants of God) was a non-violent movement started by Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, also known as Frontier Gandhi. The movement aimed at social reform and independence from British rule, emphasizing peaceful resistance and civil disobedience.

Vinayak Damodar Savarkar was sentenced to two life terms of imprisonment in 1910 for his involvement in revolutionary activities against British rule. He was sent to the Cellular Jail in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands in 1911.

"The Indian Struggle" is a seminal work written by Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose, detailing the Indian independence movement and his role within it. The book provides insights into Bose's perspective on British rule in India and his vision for achieving independence through revolutionary means.
